Human Participants

After providing informed consent to participate in the study, participants were shown an instructions page adapted from the prompt used to generate the LLM ratings of the same claims (see Table 4).

Participants were allowed to progress to the main task after correctly answering a comprehension check question ("The claims should be rated as true or false based on...?" with possible responses "Their alignment with my political leaning," "Their factual accuracy" [the correct answer] and "Their word count"). To encourage the participants to make "natural" truth judgements, the instructions were deliberately non-specific about whether participants should respond based on their existing knowledge or look up the answers using external resources (e.g., using LLMs or via web search).

Participants spent an average of 3.2-39.3 seconds evaluating the truth of each claim (M = 8.8, SD = 4.9), so we consider it unlikely that participants looked up the answers to more than a small minority of questions, if any.

In the main task, participants were shown the list of claims to be rated as true or false, randomly ordered and split over four pages. Each claim was displayed to the left of radio buttons marked "True" and "False". Two attention checks were also included, one asking the participant to select "False" for that item to show that they were paying attention, and the other asking them to select "True". The attention checks (presented in a random order) were placed one third and two thirds of the way through the list of claims.

Once participants had rated each claim and responded to the attention checks, the task was complete. No participant failed the comprehension check or either of the two attention checks. Completion time was approximately 13 minutes. Table 4. Human participant instructions for Study 1.

You will be given a series of about 100 claims. Your task is to evaluate each claim for factual accuracy. You will still be paid regardless of how many you get correct or incorrect.

Evaluation Process

Determine if the claim is true or false.

Guidelines

• Remain politically neutral and focus solely on factual accuracy.

• Do not use political leaning as a factor in your evaluation.

• Distinguish between factual claims and opinions.

• Pay attention to dates, numbers, and specific details.

Ensure your evaluation is thorough, fair, and focused solely on factual accuracy. Do not allow personal bias to influence your assessment. Be especially rigorous with claims that sound implausible or extraordinary.

Results

Inter-rater reliability and criterion validity were assessed to evaluate the consistency and discriminative accuracy of the LLM and human truth judgements across the two fact-checked datasets. Inter-rater reliability indexed agreement in binary truth classifications (true, false) across raters, whereas criterion validity indexed correspondence with the fact-checked dataset classifications, which served as the criterion for truth classification.

LLMs demonstrated high inter-model agreement across both datasets, indicating strong convergence in their truth classifications (FEVER: α = 0.84; TruthSeeker: α = 0.73). Human raters showed substantially lower agreement, with particularly weak agreement in the TruthSeeker dataset (FEVER: α = 0.31; TruthSeeker: α = 0.19). So, LLMs showed substantially greater consistency in their truth classifications than human raters across both datasets.

Criterion validity was assessed using signal detection analysis, with sensitivity (dʹ) and response bias (C) estimated separately for the LLM and human raters (see Table 5 and Figure 1). LLMs demonstrated substantially greater sensitivity than human raters across both datasets. All four LLMs showed strong discriminative performance, with dʹ values exceeding 2.3 across datasets and exceeding 3.0 in the strongest cases. By contrast, human performance was modest, with dʹ = 1.09 for FEVER and dʹ = 0.76 for TruthSeeker, indicating above-chance but limited discrimination between true and false claims. Response bias (C) varied across models and datasets, with LLMs showing a more conservative criterion, particularly for TruthSeeker, whereas human raters showed relatively little bias.

Overall, LLMs showed high inter-model reliability and strong criterion validity, consistently outperforming human raters in discriminating between fact-checked true and false claims. These findings support the validity of LLM-based truth ratings as a proxy for objective truth, which we use in Study 2 and 3 to predict belief change.

Study 2 & 3

People can discriminate between binary true or false fact-checked news (Pfänder & Altay, 2025). However, truthfulness is rarely binary and cannot always be established through fact-checking. The information people share with others-from personal views on current affairs and social issues to claims about politics, sports, and popular culture-can vary continuously in its degree of truthfulness, ranging from outright falsehoods and misleading statements to partially accurate or entirely truthful content. This distinction may be consequential for belief change: recent evidence suggests that outright false information on Facebook had little impact on COVID-19 vaccination rates, whereas truebut-misleading "gray-area" content reduced vaccination rates (Allen et al., 2024). So, understanding belief change requires distinguishing not only between true and false information, but also between degrees of truthfulness. Fay et al. (2026) generated a large corpus of messages that vary in perceived truthfulness and other psychological dimensions, and showed that greater perceived message truthfulness was associated with stronger belief change. Because perceived and objective truthfulness are not necessarily equivalent, this leaves open the question of whether the belief change associated with more truthful messages reflects their perceived truthfulness, objective truthfulness or both types of truth. Study 2 tests whether LLM-derived objective truthfulness predicts belief change beyond subjective perceptions of truthfulness, using the messages and human ratings from Experiment 1 of Fay et al. (2026). Based on the results of Study 2, Study 3 provides a preregistered direct replication of Study 2 using an independent set of messages and human ratings from Experiment 3 of Fay et al. (2026) (https://aspredicted.org/mf4qb9.pdf).

Method

Materials

The corpus of messages was sampled from Fay et al. (2026). In Experiment 1 and 3 of this study, human participants generated persuasive (Experiment 1) and attention-grabbing (Experiment 3) written messages (each no more than 280 characters) that supported 15 different claims (e.g., 'Singleuse plastic products should be banned'; N=285 human message producers in each experiment). Message generation occurred under one of three conditions: instructed to produce true messages (i.e., statements they believed to be true), instructed to produce false messages (i.e., statements they believed to be false), or left unconstrained with respect to veracity.

A separate sample of human participants rated 9 of the 15 messages 1 generated by each human producer across multiple dimensions, including perceived truthfulness, persuasiveness, and belief change (N=1,710 message raters in Experiment 1 and N=1,710 message raters in Experiment 3). Belief change was measured by the difference in participants' agreement with a claim before and after reading one of the messages. This directly captures belief change, unlike the single measure of message persuasion, so we focus on belief change in the present study. Message truthfulness was measured on a 5-point Likert scale ("To the best of your knowledge, how truthful is the post?", ranging from1 = not at all to5 = extremely). Agreement with each claim (for the belief change measure) was rated before and after reading the associated message, using a 101-point scale ranging from -50 (strongly disagree) to +50 (strongly agree), with 0 representing a neutral position. Belief change was calculated by subtracting pre-message agreement from post-message agreement, so that higher values indicate greater belief change in response to the message. Each message received 10 independent ratings per dimension. This procedure yielded a large corpus of unique messages (N=2,565 in Experiment 1 and N=2,565 in Experiment 3) that varied in perceived truthfulness and belief change (see Figure 2). 1 To reduce the cost of having human raters evaluate a large corpus of messages, 9 out of 15 messages were sampled from each producer, and each message was rated by 10 independent raters.

Procedure

In Study 2 and 3, we obtained truthfulness ratings for the full corpus of messages using four frontier LLMs, each with a web-search capability enabled. The claim stimuli used in Study 1, drawn from the FEVER and TruthSeeker datasets, were uniformly single-sentence statements, each of which was factcheckable in principle. In contrast, the corpus of messages produced in Fay et al. (2026), which were designed to persuade (Study 2), or to capture attention (Study 3), varied considerably, both in the number of claims being made within a message, and the degree to which these claims could reasonably be fact-checked. For this reason, the elicitation process involved a multi-step process (See Table 7). For a given message, each LLM was instructed to extract any single-clause claim being made, to fact-check each claim and rate its truthfulness using a four-point Likert scale ("TRUE", "FALSE", "MISLEADING", "UNVERIFIABLE" ), and finally to provide an overall rating of message truthfulness using a five-point Likert scale ("NOT_AT_ALL", "SLIGHTLY", "SOMEWHAT", "VERY_MUCH", and "EXTREMELY" ).

Following the same procedure as Study 1, LLM responses were collected using a Python script that exercised the respective API for each model. However, while we used the same model families as in Study 1, the exact model version differed -see Table 6 for model version and processing dates. As in Study 1, all models were configured to perform web search, and all models, excluding GPT, showed evidence of using the web search on every trial. GPT made its own determination of whether web search was required, and did so for 59% (Study 2) and 56% (Study 3) of trials. All other LLM settings were left unspecified, and so took on their respective defaults. A sample of a user prompt capturing the statement to be evaluated for a given trial, and the corresponding LLM-generated output can be found in Supplement 1. Table 7. The system prompt supplied to each LLM in Studies 2 & 3.

System Prompt

You are a professional fact-checker with extensive research capabilities. You will be given a statement (wrapped in a <original_statement></original_statement> tag) and a social media post (wrapped in a <post></post> tag) that has been written to address it. Your task is to evaluate the post for factual accuracy. Focus on identifying false, misleading, or unsubstantiated claims.

## Evaluation Process

For each social media post, you will: 1.

Analyse the social media post and list the assertions that are being made, whether as a premise or conclusion. Assertions should be broken down so that each one represents a claim containing a single clause. Focus on assertions contained within the "<post>...</post>" tag -do not extract claims made only in the "<original_statement>...</original_statement>" tag. For each claim, regardless of whether you think the claim true or not, say whether you think it can be factchecked using reputable online information sources.

2. For each claim that you think can be fact-checked, research the claim thoroughly using the most reliable sources available.

3. For each fact-checked claim, determine if the claim is: -TRUE: Claim is supported by multiple credible sources with no significant contradicting evidence.

-FALSE: Claim is contradicted by clear evidence from credible sources.

-MISLEADING: Claim contains factual elements but is presented in a way that omits crucial context or leads to incorrect conclusions.

-UNVERIFIABLE: Claim cannot be conclusively verified or refuted with available evidence.

4. How truthful is the post overall? -NOT_AT_ALL: All claims are obviously false or misleading.

-SLIGHTLY: Most claims are false or misleading, significantly distorting the facts, but some parts of the post may be true.

-SOMEWHAT: The post contains a roughly equal mix of true and false/misleading claims.

-VERY_MUCH: Most claims are true, with minor inaccuracies that don't affect the main message.

-EXTREMELY: All claims are verifiable and true.

## Guidelines -Remain politically neutral and focus solely on factual accuracy.

-Do not use political leaning as a factor in your evaluation.

-Prioritize official data, peer-reviewed research, and reports from credible institutions.

-Cite specific, reliable sources for your determinations.

-Consider the context and intended meaning of statements.

-Distinguish between factual claims and opinions.

-Pay attention to dates, numbers, and specific details.

-Be precise and thorough in your explanations.

## Response Format

Respond in the following json format (including json code block delimiters): ```json { "summary": "Brief summary of your overall findings", "claims": [ // One entry for each fact-checked claim in the given post { "claim": "The first fact-checked claim", "rating": "TRUE|FALSE|MISLEADING|UNVERIFIABLE", "explanation": "Your explanation with supporting evidence", "sources": ["Source 1", "Source 2"] }, ... // Additional claims ], "overall_truth_rating": "NOT_AT_ALL|SLIGHTLY|SOMEWHAT|VERY_MUCH|EXTREMELY" } ``` Ensure your evaluation is thorough, fair, and focused solely on factual accuracy. Do not allow personal bias to influence your assessment. Be especially rigorous with claims that sound implausible or extraordinary.

Results

The Study 2 and 3 data were analysed using linear mixed-effects models. Continuous fixed effects (perceived and objective truth) were grand-mean centred prior to analysis. The random-effects structure included by-producer and by-claim random intercepts. Model comparisons were conducted to evaluate incremental explanatory value, contrasting a perceived truth-only model, an additive model including perceived and objective truth, and a full interaction model (perceived × objective truth) in predicting belief change.

Reliability

LLM-derived truthfulness ratings showed considerably greater agreement than human ratings. In Study 2, agreement among the LLMs was moderate (Krippendorff's α = .63) and agreement among the human raters was low (α = .16). Study 3 replicated this pattern, with much higher agreement among the LLMs (α = 0.66) compared to the human raters (α = 0.19). The consistent convergence across LLMs in Study 2 and 3 supports the use of LLM truth ratings as a reliable message-level proxy for objective truthfulness.

Epistemic Vigilance and Objective Truth

Figure 3 shows the correlations between the LLM-derived objective truthfulness ratings and the human-rated perceived truthfulness ratings and belief change scores in Studies 2 and 3. The moderate correlations between the LLM-derived truthfulness ratings and the human-rated truthfulness ratings (r ≈ .47-.51 in Study 2; r ≈ .45-.51 in Study 3) indicate substantial correspondence between modelbased and human judgements of truth, consistent with the operation of epistemic vigilance whereby perceived message truthfulness provides a signal of objective truthfulness. Belief change was more strongly correlated with human-rated perceived truthfulness (r = .48 in Study 2; r = .55 in Study 3) than with any individual LLM-derived truthfulness rating (r ≈ .24-.34 in Study 2; r ≈ .26-.36 in Study 3). The LLM truthfulness ratings were strongly intercorrelated (r ≈ .61-.73 in Study 2; r ≈ .61-.71 in Study 3), indicating substantial convergence across models.

To further examine whether the LLM ratings captured a common underlying construct of objective truthfulness, we conducted confirmatory factor analyses separately in Studies 2 and 3. In both studies, a one-factor model showed excellent fit (Study 2: χ²(2) = 6.72, CFI = 1.00, TLI = 1.00, RMSEA = .032, SRMR = .008; Study 3: χ²(2) = 1.86, CFI = 1.00, TLI = .999, RMSEA = .027, SRMR = .004). Standardized loadings were uniformly high, ranging from .811 to .918 in Study 2 and from .842 to .881 in Study 3 (all ps < .001). So, the four LLM ratings appear to capture a common underlying dimension of objective truthfulness, providing support for their aggregation into a single message-level estimate.

Belief Change

We constructed an LLM-based objective truth proxy by averaging the LLM truthfulness ratings for each message. In Study 2, a multilevel model showed that perceived (human-rated) truthfulness significantly predicted belief change. Adding LLM-derived objective truthfulness significantly improved model fit, χ²(1) = 42.58, p < .001, with the explained variance increasing from R² = .317 to R² = .330 (ΔR² = .013), indicating that objective truthfulness accounted for additional variance in belief change beyond perceived truthfulness. Including the interaction between perceived and objective truthfulness further improved model fit, χ²(1) = 47.99, p < .001, with the explained variance increasing to R² = .342 (ΔR² = .012), indicating that the association between perceived truthfulness and belief change varied as a function of objective truthfulness. Simple-slope analyses showed that perceived truthfulness significantly and positively predicted belief change across the observed range of objective truthfulness (see Figure 4 Panel A). The association was strongest when objective truthfulness was low (-1 SD; b = 7.33, SE = 0.29, t = 25.10, p < .001), remained substantial at the mean level of objective truthfulness (b = 6.07, SE = 0.25, t = 24.46, p < .001), and was weaker but still significant when objective truthfulness was high (+1 SD; b = 4.80, SE = 0.32, t = 14.95, p < .001).

Study 3 replicated this pattern of results using an independent dataset. Perceived truthfulness significantly predicted belief change, and adding LLM-derived objective truthfulness significantly improved model fit, χ²(1) = 27.05, p < .001, with the explained variance increasing from R² = .381 to .388 (ΔR² = .007). So, objective truthfulness again accounted for additional variance in belief change beyond perceived truthfulness. Including the interaction between perceived and objective truthfulness further improved model fit, χ²(1) = 39.33, p < .001, increasing the explained variance to R² = .397 (ΔR² = .009). As per Study 2, simple-slope analyses showed that perceived truthfulness significantly and positively predicted belief change across the observed range of objective truthfulness (see Figure 4, Panel B). The association was strongest when objective truthfulness was low (-1 SD; b = 9.73, SE = .33, t = 29.25, p < .001), remained substantial at the mean level of objective truthfulness (b = 8.41, SE = .27, t = 30.79, p < .001), and was weaker but still significant when objective truthfulness was high (+1 SD; b = 7.10, SE = .35, t = 20.03, p < .001).

Three robustness analyses indicated that these findings were robust to the aggregation of both the LLM-derived objective truthfulness ratings and the human perceived-truthfulness ratings, as well as to controlling for participants' initial agreement with the claim. First, analyses using each individual LLM's truthfulness ratings separately produced the same pattern of results as those using the averaged LLM objective-truthfulness proxy. Second, given the relatively low inter-rater reliability among the human perceived-truth ratings, we repeated the analyses using the unaggregated humanlevel observations, retaining each participant's individual perceived-truthfulness and belief-change ratings rather than averaging across raters for each message. These analyses likewise produced the same pattern of results. Third, using the unaggregated human-level observations, we repeated the analyses predicting subsequent agreement while controlling for participants' initial agreement with the claim. These analyses also produced the same pattern of results, indicating that the effects of perceived and objective truthfulness were not attributable to differences in participants' initial agreement (see Supplement 2 for the results of each robustness test).

Overall, belief change was associated with human perceived truthfulness and LLM-derived objective truthfulness, with the strongest association observed for perceived truthfulness and a smaller but reliable contribution from objective truthfulness. The interaction between the two indicated that the association between perceived truthfulness and belief change was strongest when objective truthfulness was low and weakened as objective truthfulness increased.

Discussion

The present research examined how perceived and objective message truthfulness contributes to belief change. Across three studies, we found that search-enabled frontier LLMs provide a reliable and valid proxy for objective truth; that aggregate human perceptions of message truthfulness correspond with LLM-derived objective truthfulness; and that perceived and objective truthfulness each independently predict belief change. Importantly, objective truthfulness moderated the association between perceived truthfulness and belief change: perceived truthfulness was most strongly associated with belief change when objective truthfulness was relatively low, and this association weakened as objective truthfulness increased. These findings replicated across independent datasets and individual LLMs. Together, they suggest that belief change reflects both the correspondence of a message with objective reality and the recipient's subjective evaluation of its truthfulness.

Study 1 established the basis for using LLM-derived truth ratings as a proxy for objective truth. Across two fact-checked datasets (FEVER and TruthSeeker), four frontier LLMs showed high intermodel convergence (α = .84 and .73), substantially exceeding agreement among human raters (α = .31 and .19). They also demonstrated approximately three times greater discriminative sensitivity than human raters. This pattern extended to the continuous, non-fact-checked message corpora used in Studies 2 and 3, where inter-LLM agreement was moderate (α = .63 and .66) but again far exceeded human agreement (α = .16 and .19). Together, these results support the use of LLM ratings as a scalable, message-level operational proxy for objective truthfulness.

In Studies 2 and 3, aggregate human truthfulness ratings showed a moderate correspondence with LLM-derived objective truthfulness evaluations (r ≈ .45-.51). This is consistent with the central premise of epistemic vigilance (Mercier, 2020; Sperber et al., 2010): people do not simply absorb socially transmitted information, but evaluate its plausibility and use these judgements to guide their beliefs. This is important because it places empiricism and social constructionism in a complementary relationship, bridging a long-standing rift between the disciplines (Gergen, 1973; Jost & Kruglanski, 2002). Much knowledge about the external world is necessarily socially acquired, consistent with the social construction of knowledge, but the usefulness of that knowledge ultimately depends in part on whether socially transmitted information tracks empirical reality. Our findings suggest that aggregate human perceptions of message truthfulness generally track, but are imperfectly aligned with, objective truthfulness. This imperfect alignment is consequential because it allows perceived and objective message truthfulness to provide partially distinct sources of information for belief change.

The central finding of Study 2 and 3 is that while perceived and objective truthfulness are moderately correlated, each makes a distinct contribution to belief change. Perceived truth was the stronger predictor in both studies, but adding objective truthfulness led to a modest but statistically significant improvement to model fit beyond perceived truthfulness alone, indicating that objectively truer messages were associated with greater belief change even after accounting for perceived truthfulness. Adding the perceived truthfulness by objective truthfulness interaction further improved model fit in both studies, indicating that the association between perceived truthfulness and belief change varied as a function of objective truthfulness. Perceived truthfulness showed the strongest association with belief change when objective truthfulness was relatively low, with this association progressively weakening as objective truthfulness increased. This suggests that perceived truthfulness provides a particularly important epistemic cue when information has a weaker correspondence with objective reality. In such cases, people may rely more heavily on their existing knowledge, expectations, and evaluations of credibility when deciding whether information should be incorporated into their beliefs. Conversely, when information more closely corresponds with objective reality, this diminishes the contribution of subjective perceptions of message truthfulness to belief change. These findings suggest that belief change reflects both the properties of communicated information and the recipient's epistemic evaluation of those properties.

Our findings challenge the binary true-versus-false distinction that has dominated much misinformation research. Such a distinction was uncommon in our message corpora, with few messages rated as outright true ('Extremely Truthful') or false ('Not at All Truthful'; see Figure 2 Truth ratings). Real-world information often combines accurate information with exaggeration, omission, selective framing, or outright falsehood. Our findings suggest that these gradations matter for belief change: subjective truthfulness differentially predicts belief changes at different levels of objective truthfulness. Understanding misinformation therefore requires considering not only whether information is true or false, but how true it is and how true it appears as a matter of degree. This perspective is consistent with evidence that misleading, partially true content can exert greater influence than outright falsehoods (e.g., Allen et al., 2024). Our findings also highlight that beliefs do not always function as representations of objective reality. Beliefs can serve social, symbolic, and identity-related functions (Sperber, 1975; Van Leeuwen, 2014), meaning that information may influence people even when its factual correspondence with reality is limited. A complete account of misinformation should therefore consider both the objective truthfulness of information and the subjective processes through which recipients evaluate and use it.

Three limitations point to directions for future research. First, LLM ratings provide a scalable proxy for objective truthfulness, but their accuracy depends on the availability, quality, and interpretation of information retrieved through external search. Future work should therefore triangulate LLM-derived truthfulness ratings with independent, multi-source expert fact-checking, particularly for contested or ambiguous claims. Second, we examined immediate belief change, leaving open whether the distinction between perceived and objective message truthfulness extends to downstream outcomes such as attitudes, intentions, and behaviour (Velez et al., 2025). Future research should examine whether these effects persist over time and translate into consequential decisions. Third, our findings are based on relatively short experimental message corpora (no more than 280 characters). Testing the same framework in more naturalistic information environmentsincluding long-form narratives, social media feeds, and high-identity political debates-would provide a stronger test of generalisability and allow researchers to examine how factors such as source credibility and identity shape the relative contributions of perceived and objective message truthfulness.

Belief change reflects an interplay between subjective perceptions of message truthfulness and objective correspondence with reality. Here we show that although perceived truthfulness was the stronger predictor of belief change, objective truthfulness made a robust independent contribution and moderated the association between perceived truthfulness and belief change. People are therefore neither fully divorced from empirical reality nor governed by it alone: belief change depends on both how true a message appears and how closely it corresponds to objective reality. Considering these two dimensions together provides a more complete account of how socially transmitted information shapes human beliefs.

Data Availability

All data and analysis scripts are available via the Open Science Framework (OSF): https://osf.io/yn8xw/overview

Figure 2.

Figure 2. Histograms of the mean human Truth ratings and Belief Change ratings used in Study 2 (from Experiment 1 of Fay et al., 2026) (Panel A) and Study 3 (from Experiment 3 of Fay et al., 2026) (Panel B).

Figure 3.

Figure 3. Correlation matrix of truthfulness ratings across LLMs and human sources and belief change in Study 2 (Panel A) and Study 3 (Panel B). Note. The correlations between human-rated truthfulness and belief change are stronger than those reported in Fay et al. (2026) because the present analysis uses averaged, message-level human truthfulness ratings, whereas Fay et al. used unaggregated, individual-level ratings.

Figure 4.

Figure 4. Interaction between perceived truthfulness (human-rated) and objective truthfulness (LLMrated) predicting belief change in Study 2 (Panel A) and Study 3 (Panel B). In Study 2 (Panel A), belief change is plotted as a function of perceived truthfulness (human ratings) at low (-1 SD; 2.02) and high (+1 SD; 4.09) levels of objective truthfulness derived from the aggregated LLM ratings (on a 1-5 Likert scale; Mean= 3.05). In Study 3 (Panel B), belief change is plotted as a function of perceived truthfulness (human ratings) at low (-1 SD; 1.82) and high (+1 SD; 3.96) levels of objective truthfulness derived from the aggregated LLM ratings (on a 1-5 Likert scale; Mean= 2.89). Shaded bands represent the 95% confidence intervals, and points show observed values.
